lines.text: Every rainy season, communities along the Ogun River face the same question. Will the water reach us this time?

In June twenty twenty-six, satellite records show rainfall over Ogun State forty-one percent above normal. Downstream of the Oyan Dam, in places like Isheri, Akute and Magboro, residents have been urged to move to higher ground.
Yet the people most affected rarely have a clear picture of where the risk lies, or of what is happening on the ground.
FloodSense brings two kinds of intelligence together. Geographic analysis of the land itself, and verified reports from the community.
This is the FloodSense map. All twenty local government areas of Ogun State, built from open satellite data.
From the Copernicus elevation model, we traced how water flows across the state. Every channel, ordered by size.
Six factors. Height above the nearest stream, distance to a channel, slope, wetness, rainfall and land cover. They are weighted using the Analytic Hierarchy Process, to map flood susceptibility.
Tap any location, and FloodSense explains why it scores the way it does. Here, beside the Ogun River in Ifo, the ground sits less than a metre above the river channel.
We checked the model against thirty-seven years of Landsat water observations. The highest class covers eleven percent of the land, but holds seventy-three percent of the water ever observed.
Now, a resident sees flooding in their street. They open FloodSense on their phone, drop a pin, choose how severe it is, describe what they see, and send.
The report reaches the map straight away, but only as pending. Its text stays hidden, and its location is blurred, until someone checks it.
Because not every report is accurate, trained verifiers review each one. FloodSense shows them the terrain at that exact spot, nearby reports, and automatic spam checks.
Once verified, the report is published, and the dashboard updates directly from the database.
Planners can test their own assumptions, re-weighting the model and recalculating the whole state in seconds.
FloodSense does not forecast floods. It connects what the land tells us with what communities see, so that residents, local governments and emergency managers can prepare before the water rises.
Floods may be difficult to prevent, but better information can help communities prepare. With FloodSense, we are bringing geographic intelligence closer to the people who need it.
